Anna —

Attached are the materials we discussed. Short summary included below; full PDF and diagrams are attached. Let us know if you prefer a short walkthrough call.

Executive summary (short):
- Deployment surfaces: Hosted (multi-tenant logically isolated, per-request auth & tenant IDs), Dedicated (per-customer reserved pools with hardware isolation and private networking), Private (VPC/on-prem with customer-controlled networking and optional air-gap).
- Network segregation: control-plane (management API) is logically separated from data-plane; data-plane endpoints require per-tenant mTLS and token-based auth. For Dedicated and Private, customer traffic remains on private network links whenever configured.
- Routing & fallbacks: policy engine evaluates latency, cost, and capacity. Fallbacks are strictly gated and observability flags raise alerts; fallbacks can be disabled per-customer by policy.

Threat scenarios (abridged):
1) Initial access: phishing -> compromised developer credentials. Mitigations: MFA, short-lived service tokens, dev environment segmentation, RBAC with least privilege, and audit trail retention.
2) Lateral movement: attacker tries to reach Dedicated GPU pools from Hosted plane. Mitigations: strict tenant network ACLs, enforcement at hypervisor/namespace boundary, no cross-tenant default routes, flow logs and anomaly detection, automated containment playbooks.
3) Data exfiltration: attacker attempts to pull model cache / KVS contents. Mitigations: application-level encryption of KV cache, per-customer KMS keys, egress filtering, DLP hooks on export endpoints, and sampling-based model hallucination detection to detect exfil attempts.

Attachments: redwood-deployment-zones-v1.pdf, network-segmentation-diagram-v2.png, threat-model-briefing-ACME.docx

Subject: Re: Deliverable: deployment zones + threat summary — addendum

Hi Anna —

Quick addendum to answer your two questions:

1) KV cache replication: By design, KV cache used for active inference is scoped per-runtime surface and per-tenant. We do not replicate customer KV caches across Hosted/Dedicated/Private surfaces. When a request is routed across surfaces (policy fallback), we do not transfer raw KV entries; instead we rely on a rehydration mechanism that pulls authoritative data from customer-specific persistent storage (encrypted at rest) and re-creates transient caches in the target runtime. This avoids cross-surface cache leakage.

2) SOC 2 egress control: Egress filtering is implemented as a combination of network-level ACLs at the subnet/host route level (documented in our SOC 2 controls mapping) plus application-layer egress policies enforced by the gateway. Customer-configurable egress allowlists are supported for Dedicated and Private deployments; Hosted customers may request contractually-managed egress restrictions. SOC 2 reports and the control-mapping are available under NDA; we can post the control IDs to your secure Drive link.

Procurement safe-phrase to disable fallbacks: "Redwood shall not route traffic from Customer workloads to any non-dedicated runtime surface without Customer’s explicit written authorization."

If that works I’ll append to the PDF and push a version to the Drive link.

Thanks,
Naomi Feldman
Senior Security Architect
Redwood Inference
